title: Pierre Andurand on How We Might Get $200 a Barrel Oil - Odd Lots

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/Pierre Andurand on How We Might Get $200 a Barrel Oil - Odd Lots.docx

summary: Odd Lots interview (10 March 2022) with commodity hedge fund manager Pierre Andurand on the Russia-Ukraine oil shock. Approach: fundamental supply, demand and inventory balances, backwardation and storage as tightness gauges, long options for big moves. Conclusions: oil up to about $200 needed to destroy demand, supply response is slow (shale 12 months, metals 7-15 years), sanctions will persist, commodities cap growth for a decade.

completeness_estimate: 0.82 - first reader caught the main causal chains, numbers and market views; missed secondary mechanisms (self-limiting shale response, Iran priced in, metals lead-time detail, mandates scale, instrument and holding-period details)

claims.speaker: Joe Weisenthal
claims.quote: within the last week we both had the biggest update for the bloomberg commodity spot index since 2008 and the biggest down day
claims.claim: In March 2022 the Bloomberg Commodity Spot Index had its biggest up day and biggest down day since 2008, and oil spiked almost 20% then fell almost 20%, showing extreme volatility.
claims.indicator: Bloomberg Commodity Spot Index, oil daily moves
claims.conditions: war-driven commodity shock, March 2022

claims.speaker: Joe Weisenthal
claims.quote: you have the combination of an extremely tight market across the board combined with geopolitical events that of course are inherently uncertain non-linear and unpredictable
claims.claim: Commodity volatility is highest when tight physical markets meet non-linear geopolitical shocks.
claims.conditions: tight inventories plus geopolitical event

claims.speaker: Tracy Alloway
claims.quote: sometimes you know sort of um canceling trades which is something we saw from the london metal exchange
claims.claim: In extreme volatility exchanges can cancel trades (the LME did with nickel) and financing and physical delivery constraints appear, adding execution and counterparty risk.
claims.conditions: extreme volatility, margin and settlement stress

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: it's a market that's driven by geopolitical events there's been a lot of reading trying to understand you know how the war will pan out
claims.claim: In a geopolitically driven market, the work is reading how the war and sanctions will evolve, and calls are hard to make with confidence.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: already with very low inventories with the low speed capacity in the hands of opec and in general low production capacity spare production capacity a low expected supply growth and high expected demand goals
claims.claim: Before the invasion, oil already had very low inventories, little OPEC spare capacity, low expected supply growth and strong post-Covid demand, so fundamentals were very strong independent of Russia.
claims.conditions: pre-invasion, early 2022
claims.testable: yes - inventory and spare capacity data

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: backwardation means the front end the first contracts are much higher than the back contracts and and it means that the market is very tight physically
claims.claim: Backwardation (front contracts above deferred) measures physical tightness; Brent backwardation was about $2 a month before the invasion and $4-5 after, with gasoil above $50 a barrel between two months.
claims.conditions: tight physical market

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: there haven't been like massive disruptions yet it's just the fears of how the sanctions will bite that that keeps the market tight
claims.claim: Prices were already high on fear of sanctions before actual supply loss, so the move could be the beginning or the end, which makes strong calls difficult.
claims.conditions: early in a geopolitical shock

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: study the fundamentals of the market studies the growth of demand relative to the growth of supply and as a result uh you know have an idea if inventories are going to go up on or down
claims.claim: Process: model demand growth versus supply growth to project inventory direction and the price needed to balance the market so storage or inventory limits are not breached.
claims.direction: long when inventories fall, short when they build

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: so for me i'm trying to make money from the large moves in the old market
claims.claim: Andurand is directionally agnostic: he has been short (late 2008, 2014-15, before Covid) and long, seeking the large oil moves that last months to years.
claims.direction: long or short large oil trends

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: we don't sell options we either flat options or long options
claims.claim: Andurand never sells options; he is flat or long calls and puts, so risk is capped at premium.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: when when we feel like the market is going to you know make a big move in a short period of time then we prefer to be to express that view with options relative to futures
claims.claim: When expecting a big move in a short period he expresses the view with long options rather than futures, getting more leverage with less risk.
claims.conditions: expected large short-term move
claims.testable: partly - option vs futures payoff testable

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: it's really important to understand the physical because it's what's going to drive the price of oil
claims.claim: Understanding physical inventories, storage and delivery mechanics is essential even for a futures-only trader because physical balance drives price.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: the level of uh empty storage was um enough was actually could only take one and a half months of this really low demand before all the tanks were full
claims.claim: In April 2020 demand fell 20% overnight and empty storage could absorb only about 1.5 months of surplus, after which unstorable oil drove prices negative.
claims.conditions: demand collapse

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: if somebody is long futures and try to take delivery of of oil at that at that place and that point in time well nobody can deliver and then you can go to any price
claims.claim: The mirror case: with empty tanks at delivery points such as Cushing, a long who stands for delivery cannot be filled and price can spike without limit.
claims.direction: long oil when delivery stocks are depleted
claims.conditions: very low inventories

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: the price should move in order to keep the the inventories within kind of uh kind of in range that makes the market function
claims.claim: The role of speculators is price discovery: prices must move enough to keep inventories between empty and full, and if they lag prices later have to overshoot.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: now u.s shell has been producing you know at scale for 10 years and there's still room you know for another you know 10 years of also of strong supply
claims.claim: US shale has already drilled much of the easy oil and fields are maturing, so about 10 more years of strong supply is possible but not decades of high growth.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: the whole industry had burned through 600 billion dollars of cash and the shareholders had taken a big hit
claims.claim: US shale producers burned about $600 billion of cash while growing production, so shareholders lost heavily.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: the shareholders of those companies pressure the the ceos to not grow production too fast because if they grow it too fast then prices crash again
claims.claim: Now profitable, shale producers face shareholder and climate pressure to keep capital discipline, which limits the supply response to high prices.
claims.direction: higher prices needed, supply response muted

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: there hasn't been a lot of work in giving a solution for the consumers right to have another choice but to buy oil
claims.claim: Pressure on oil supply to fall has outrun alternatives for consumers, so oil demand cannot shift quickly and shortages result.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: there's not enough power to charge those evs so we will have an issue at least in europe in finding a solution for for power supply
claims.claim: Replacing combustion cars with EVs is limited by grid power supply, especially in Europe, which slows decarbonization of oil demand.
claims.conditions: Europe

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: the growth of supply in metals is not going to be large enough to build as many evs and to electrify the world as fast as we'd like because the miners have not invested enough
claims.claim: Metal supply is too small for fast electrification because miners underinvested under ESG pressure, and renewables, batteries and EVs are copper-intensive.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: metals prices will have to go up a lot in order to incentivize enough supply growth to be able to decarbonize the world
claims.claim: Decarbonization needs much higher metals prices to induce the supply growth required.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: they will not do it before they understand that the russian oil is out and will not come back in time soon
claims.claim: Gulf producers (Saudi, Kuwait) and the US could add about 1.5 mb/d but only after Russian supply is visibly gone, not preemptively, against a potential 4 mb/d loss.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: i still think that the sanctions will stay on russia until the west can feel like they can trust them
claims.claim: Sanctions would stay until the West trusts Russia again, which Andurand thinks requires regime change, so Russian oil would not return quickly even after a ceasefire.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: even though we don't have formal sanctions yet from the eu in practice not everybody can buy oil
claims.claim: Self-sanctioning by refiners, insurers and banks (no insurance for ships, no letters of credit even from Chinese banks) restricts Russian oil sales before formal sanctions.
claims.indicator: Russian oil sales, insurance and letters of credit
claims.conditions: private-sector self-sanctioning
claims.testable: partly - discount of Urals to Brent

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: russia will have to stop production because they will run out of storage capacity at their ports and and and so basically they will need to cut production by two at least two million bars a day
claims.claim: If Russian cargoes cannot be sold, port storage fills within weeks and Russia must shut in 2-3 mb/d, which takes time to restore.
claims.conditions: if buyers stay away

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: making europe is very dependent on russian gas gas has been natural gas mainly germany and italy
claims.claim: Europe, especially Germany and Italy, depends on Russian gas and may ration demand and accelerate the energy transition, which in turn needs metals.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: they could release up to 5 million barrels a day for 12 months
claims.claim: Strategic petroleum reserves of IEA members can release up to 5 mb/d for 12 months (about 2 mb/d for 2.5 years) but leave reserves empty and need refilling.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: or it will have to be coming from price and then the price will have to be high enough to bring that demand down by one and a half million bucks a day also
claims.claim: After SPR and Gulf supply, about 1.5 mb/d (roughly 2%) of demand must be destroyed through government mandates or price.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: you don't really generally have such thing as demand destruction for oil because you can't really replace in the short term right
claims.claim: Short-run oil demand is inelastic because consumers cannot replace cars quickly, so demand destruction comes from economic crises, not price alone.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: maybe they'll use their cars a bit less for one or two months and then they'll get used to the new price
claims.claim: A price spike only slows driving for one or two months before consumers adapt, so it is not real demand destruction.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: what brings demand down that's when we have large recessions so not small recessions but large recessions
claims.claim: Oil prices fall when large recessions cut demand, not small ones, so the price level at which demand falls depends on the economic environment.
claims.conditions: large recessions only
claims.testable: yes - oil demand vs recession size

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: at the time we didn't see that demand was being hit but when le mans went burst
claims.claim: In 2008 oil reached $147 (about $200 today) without hurting demand until Lehman failed and the credit and trade-finance collapse crushed demand.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: and the economy could you know handle 150 dollars of today's dollars for for three and a half years
claims.claim: Brent averaged $110 (about $150 today) from 2011 to mid-2014 despite the euro crisis, showing the economy tolerates high real oil prices for years.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: i was expecting already prices to go above 150 before the russian invasion
claims.claim: Andurand expected oil above $150 before the invasion; the move was accelerated, not caused, by Russia.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: that the market doesn't believe that um we will lose this oil for very long
claims.claim: Brent at only $114 implies the market assumes the Russian outage is short, which is a mispricing relative to Andurand's view.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: then i think that uh around 200 oil will be enough to to bring demand down to balance the market
claims.claim: Absent mandates, oil around $200 would be needed to bring demand into balance; there is no demand destruction at $110, and 200 is possible within the year.
claims.conditions: no government mandates

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: they collectively you know agreed to cut production by around 10 million barrels a day
claims.claim: OPEC+ cut 10 mb/d in April 2020 and stayed compliant for over a year, restoring supply only gradually, which prevented a larger collapse.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: quite a few countries in opec plus could not meet dakota many of the african countries they could not produce as much as what they were allowed to because of under investment
claims.claim: Many OPEC+ members, especially African ones, cannot fill quotas because of underinvestment, so quota increases do not translate into barrels.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: i think it's probably uh only saudi kuwait and uae and that's pretty much it
claims.claim: Real spare production capacity (sustainable for 1-2 years) is only about 1.5 mb/d and sits with Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and the UAE.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: that will take you know 12 months also for for the u.s to be able to bring higher levels of supply than what is expected today
claims.claim: A US supply response above current expectations needs about 12 months, so near-term balances stay tight.
claims.testable: yes - rig count to output lag

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: i think basically if a country had a currency backed to gold or something well the western world could still sanction that currency even if it's backed by gold
claims.claim: Gold-backed or crypto-based currency does not protect against sanctions because reserves can be frozen, so the dollar's reserve status is not easily displaced.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: currencies in general it's always going to be countries that have a strong rule of law and and trust and a strong financial market that will be able to have a strong currency
claims.claim: Strong currencies need rule of law, low corruption, freedom and deep financial markets, which China lacks as it holds large US Treasuries and capital controls.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: what we need is to be able to eat and move so it's energy it's energy it's agricultural products it's food it's metal
claims.claim: To protect against high inflation, hold real needs (energy, agricultural products, metals) rather than crypto.
claims.conditions: high inflation
claims.testable: yes - commodity returns in inflation regimes

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: most of the pension funds don't have a box saying we have to be long commodities
claims.claim: Pension funds have no commodity allocation, so as commodities become important more investment flow should come, funding supply.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: for agricultural products it's pretty fast like within a year you can change things but for metals it takes anywhere between seven and fifteen years
claims.claim: Supply response time differs: agriculture within a year, metals 7-15 years, and new oil projects about 7 years, so long-lead supply cannot fix near-term shortages.
claims.direction: long metals and oil in shortage

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: for any any new projects generally today would bring oil uh supply in seven years time
claims.claim: New non-shale oil projects take about 7 years, and hesitation about demand in 2029-30 discourages long-lead investment.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: only the u.s has a shorter cycle of probably 12 months before the decision to increase capex and getting more oil
claims.claim: Only US shale responds within about a year to higher prices, so supply additions come from the US first and the rest later.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: over the next 10 years commodities are gonna cap the community's supply actually not only price but level of supply will actually cap the type of economic growth we will be able to have
claims.claim: Over the next decade commodity supply, not just price, will constrain economic growth; economic models that assume unlimited commodity supply are wrong.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: once we get less supply of any other commodities and also very low unemployment number you know it's hard to find the people
claims.claim: Bottlenecks in other commodities (steel, sand), labour shortages and low unemployment hinder new oil supply, so tight markets reinforce each other.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: this time we might not have it
claims.claim: Unlike 2008-2011, when shale then helped, there may be no equivalent supply response now, so the current setup is more bullish than 2008.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: so 150 dollars then is 220 today in today's dollars
claims.claim: In global GDP deflator terms $150 in 2008 equals about $220 today, so record nominal prices understate real stretch.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: they get used to higher levels over time
claims.claim: Consumers complain at $100, $120, $140 but adapt, so demand adjusts only slowly through marginal usage like shorter trips; recency bias makes prices look too high.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: today for one unit of gdp we're used we are using 15 less oil than in in 2008
claims.claim: Oil use per unit of GDP is 15% lower than in 2008, so the economic impact of $150 in 2008 is closer to that of about $250 today.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: i think it's a new territory i can't speak of an event that was similar over the last few decades really
claims.claim: The combined shock (very tight inventories, war, sanctions and self-sanctions) has no close precedent in recent decades, so historical analogues give little guidance on how far prices can move.
claims.conditions: Applies to the March 2022 war-driven supply shock; analogue-based sizing is unreliable.
claims.testable: no - a judgement about regime novelty, not a measurable signal

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: sometimes we'll bet that prices will go up for sometimes for a few months or a few years and and sometimes we'll bet that they go down over generally a few months
claims.claim: Andurand holds bullish oil positions for months to years but bearish positions generally for a few months up to about a year, an asymmetry in the holding period of his large-move trades.
claims.direction: long oil trades run longer than short oil trades
claims.conditions: Both directions are traded; holding period is set by the size of the supply-demand imbalance.
claims.testable: partly - durations could be checked against historical oil trend lengths

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: and we'll pick like a month for example if we want to be long the front month contract
claims.claim: Bullish views are expressed through Brent, WTI, heating oil or gasoline futures with a chosen contract month: the front month for a near-term tightness view, or a deferred month (for example December Brent) for a view further along the curve.
claims.indicator: Brent / WTI / heating oil / RBOB futures, choice of contract month on the curve
claims.direction: long front month or long deferred month
claims.conditions: Choice of curve point reflects where the view on tightness sits in time.
claims.testable: yes - curve-point choice (front versus deferred) can be backtested against roll and spread returns

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: the shareholders of those companies pressure the the ceos to not grow production too fast because if they grow it too fast then prices crash again and then they can be losing money
claims.claim: The shale supply response is self-limiting because producers know that rapid output growth would crash prices again and destroy profits, so shareholders push managers to hold output growth back even when prices are high.
claims.indicator: US shale capex and production growth versus oil price
claims.direction: slower US supply growth, price stays higher for longer
claims.conditions: Holds while the industry's memory of the cash burn (about $600 billion) persists and investors demand returns.
claims.testable: partly - shale capex discipline and rig counts versus price could be tested

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: it takes time to build solar panels and windmills and to build enough evs and enough charging stations and all that
claims.claim: The decarbonization build-out (renewables, EVs, charging) is a roughly 20-year transition that cannot replace lost fossil supply overnight, so a sudden loss of Russian oil must be met by other fossil supply or by lower demand; the system is already at capacity in the short term.
claims.direction: oil stays needed in the near term, no fast substitution
claims.conditions: Short-run only; the long-run transition plan is unchanged.
claims.testable: no - qualitative statement on substitution speed

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: if there's a region change in one week i mean i think it's unlikely but you never know
claims.claim: The sanctions scenario is conditional on regime change: if a trusted government emerged quickly, Russian oil could return in a few months, but without it the supply stays out even after fighting stops, so the duration of the outage is the key swing factor for the oil price.
claims.indicator: Russian oil export availability, sanctions status
claims.direction: Russian supply returns in months only with regime change and normal relations
claims.conditions: He judges the quick regime change scenario unlikely.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: russia is a big exporter of metals so it's not it's not going to be easy
claims.claim: Accelerating the European energy transition to cut Russian gas use needs more metals, but Russia is a big metals exporter, so the sanctions shock tightens the very supply the substitution depends on.
claims.indicator: Russian metals exports, energy transition metals demand
claims.conditions: Compounds the existing metals underinvestment problem.
claims.testable: partly - metals price response to Russian supply loss could be checked

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: here if we just need to to think of bringing all demand down by two percent it's not going to be as drastic as a global lockdown
claims.claim: Demand destruction can come from government mandates rather than price: the Covid lockdown cut oil demand about 20%, whereas the shortfall now needs only about 2%, so mandates such as a few confinement days a month could close the gap without a recession.
claims.indicator: oil demand cut required (about 2% of global demand)
claims.conditions: Only if governments choose mandates; otherwise the price must rise to near $200 to clear the market.

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: we'll probably get to deal with iran bringing a million buyers a day back but that's expected by the market
claims.claim: A return of about 1 mb/d of Iranian supply is likely but already expected by the market, so it does not offset the Russian shortfall that the price still has to reflect; only unexpected supply moves prices.
claims.direction: Iran supply is priced in, no extra bearish effect
claims.conditions: Assumes a nuclear deal and sanctions relief on Iran.
claims.testable: partly - priced-in versus surprise supply could be tested around announcements

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: it's going to be at least five years before the decision when a company decides to bring the production of certain metals or minerals up and when that supply will come
claims.claim: Metals and minerals supply cannot respond for at least five years after a production decision; permitting will probably be faster at much higher prices, but there is no short-term fix for next year or two years out.
claims.indicator: metals and minerals supply lead times
claims.direction: metals prices stay high until new supply arrives
claims.conditions: Lead time shortens somewhat when prices are very high and approvals speed up.
claims.testable: partly - lead times can be measured from project data

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: i think we'll have to live with higher prices to keep you know demand down uh to keep um to to be treated a bit more as a luxury product and also to accelerate the energy transition
claims.claim: Because supply cannot respond quickly, oil prices have to stay high enough for a prolonged period to keep demand down, treating oil as a luxury product and pushing the energy transition forward.
claims.indicator: oil price level over the next few years
claims.conditions: Until non-US supply and alternatives arrive.
claims.testable: no - view on the price path

claims.speaker: Pierre Andurand
claims.quote: only the u.s has a shorter cycle of probably 12 months before the decision to increase capex and getting more oil because they know where they only have all the infrastructure
claims.claim: US shale responds fastest, about 12 months from capex decision to oil, because the wells, infrastructure and service-company capacity already exist; other supply regions lack these so respond later.
claims.indicator: US shale infrastructure and oilfield-services capacity
claims.direction: US supply is the first to rise
claims.conditions: Needs spare service capacity; bottlenecks in labour, steel and sand can slow it.
claims.testable: partly - rig counts and services capacity versus price lag could be tested

claims.speaker: Joe Weisenthal
claims.quote: even if you throw a lot of money at this problem you know you can't make the oil producers necessarily drill
claims.claim: Money cannot compress supply lead times (drilling, mines, renewables), so a large shock produces long lead times for supply to come back and keeps the market destabilized longer than financing alone would suggest.
claims.conditions: The point applies when physical capacity and time are the binding constraints rather than capital.
